title: Metals and Non-metals
content:
# Metals and Non-metals

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals
- Compare the chemical properties of metals and non-metals
- Locate metals, non-metals, and metalloids in the periodic table
- Explain the differences in terms of structure and bonding

## Introduction

Elements can be broadly classified as **metals** or **non-metals** based on their properties. About 80% of elements are metals, but non-metals include many important elements like carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen.

## Key Concepts

### Position in the Periodic Table

[DIAGRAM: Periodic table showing metals (left, shaded), non-metals (right), and metalloid staircase between them]

**Metals:**
- Left side and centre
- Groups 1, 2, transition metals
- About 80% of elements

**Non-metals:**
- Right side of the table
- Groups 5, 6, 7, 0 (mostly)
- Includes hydrogen (top left)

**Metalloids:**
- Along the "staircase" line
- B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po, At
- Have properties of both

### Physical Properties Comparison

| Property | Metals | Non-metals |
|----------|--------|------------|
| State at room temp | Mostly solid (except Hg) | Solid, liquid, or gas |
| Appearance | Shiny (lustrous) | Dull (except diamond, graphite) |
| Malleability | Malleable (can be shaped) | Brittle |
| Ductility | Ductile (can be drawn into wire) | Cannot be drawn |
| Electrical conductivity | Good conductors | Poor conductors (except graphite) |
| Thermal conductivity | Good | Poor (except diamond) |
| Melting/boiling point | Generally high | Variable (some very low) |
| Density | Generally high | Generally low |
| Sonorous | Make sound when struck | Do not |

### Chemical Properties Comparison

| Property | Metals | Non-metals |
|----------|--------|------------|
| Electron behaviour | Lose electrons | Gain or share electrons |
| Ion formation | Positive ions (cations) | Negative ions (anions) |
| Bonding with non-metals | Ionic | Covalent |
| Bonding with metals | Metallic | N/A (ionic) |
| Oxides | Basic or amphoteric | Acidic |
| Reaction with acids | Often react, produce H₂ | Usually don't react |
| Reaction with water | Some react | Most don't react |

### Explaining the Differences

**Metallic structure:**
- Positive ions in a "sea" of delocalised electrons
- Electrons can move freely → good conductors
- Layers can slide → malleable and ductile
- Strong metallic bonds → high melting points

**Non-metallic structure:**
- Simple molecules (O₂, H₂O) or giant covalent (diamond)
- No free electrons → poor conductors
- Weak intermolecular forces → low melting points (simple molecular)
- Brittle solids (cannot be shaped)

### Metal Oxides vs Non-metal Oxides

**Metal oxides are BASIC:**
$$\text{MgO} + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

- React with acids to form salt + water
- Some dissolve in water to form alkalis

**Non-metal oxides are ACIDIC:**
$$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$
$$\text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$

- React with water to form acids
- React with bases to form salt + water

### Metalloids (Semi-metals)

**Properties of metalloids:**
- Intermediate between metals and non-metals
- Often semiconductors
- May be shiny but brittle
- Conduct electricity, but not as well as metals

**Examples and uses:**
| Metalloid | Uses |
|-----------|------|
| Silicon (Si) | Computer chips, solar cells |
| Germanium (Ge) | Semiconductors, fibre optics |
| Boron (B) | Glass, ceramics |
| Arsenic (As) | Semiconductors (with Ga) |

### Summary Table

| | Metals | Metalloids | Non-metals |
|---|--------|------------|------------|
| Position | Left/centre | Staircase | Right |
| Conductivity | Good | Moderate | Poor (usually) |
| Malleability | Yes | No | No |
| Ion type | Positive | Variable | Negative |
| Oxide type | Basic | Amphoteric | Acidic |

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** An element is shiny, malleable, and conducts electricity. Predict whether it is a metal or non-metal and suggest where it might be found in the periodic table.

**Solution:**
- Shiny appearance → characteristic of metals
- Malleable → characteristic of metals
- Conducts electricity → characteristic of metals
- This element is almost certainly a **metal**
- It would be found on the **left side or centre** of the periodic table
- Could be in Groups 1, 2, or the transition metals

---

**Example 2:** Carbon dioxide is a non-metal oxide. Predict its reaction with sodium hydroxide solution.

**Solution:**
- Non-metal oxides are acidic
- CO₂ will react with the base NaOH
- Acid + Base → Salt + Water
$$\text{CO}_2 + \text{2NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
- Product is sodium carbonate and water

---

**Example 3:** Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity but most non-metals are not.

**Solution:**
**Metals:**
- Have metallic bonding
- Contain delocalised (free) electrons
- These electrons can move through the structure
- Moving electrons carry electrical charge
- Therefore, metals conduct electricity

**Non-metals:**
- Usually form simple covalent molecules
- All electrons are fixed in covalent bonds
- There are no free electrons to move
- Therefore, they cannot conduct electricity
- (Exception: graphite has delocalised electrons)

---

**Example 4:** Silicon is a metalloid. Explain what this means and why it is useful.

**Solution:**
- A metalloid has properties between metals and non-metals
- Silicon has a shiny appearance (like metals)
- But it is brittle (like non-metals)
- It conducts electricity, but not as well as metals
- This makes it a **semiconductor**
- Its conductivity increases when heated or doped with impurities
- This property is essential for computer chips
- Silicon is the basis of the electronics industry

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Thinking hydrogen is a metal because it's on the left
- **Correct:** Hydrogen is a non-metal (gas, doesn't conduct)

- **Mistake:** Thinking all non-metals are gases
- **Correct:** Non-metals can be solids (C, S, I₂), liquids (Br₂), or gases

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that graphite (carbon) conducts electricity
- **Correct:** Graphite is an exception - it has delocalised electrons

## Practice Questions

1. State three physical properties of metals. (3 marks)

2. Explain why metals are malleable but non-metals are brittle. (4 marks)

3. Classify these elements as metals, non-metals, or metalloids: Na, S, Si, Fe, Br, Ge (3 marks)

4. Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity in terms of their structure. (3 marks)

5. Sulfur dioxide is a non-metal oxide. Predict:
   a) Whether it is acidic or basic (1 mark)
   b) Its reaction with water (2 marks)
   c) Its reaction with sodium hydroxide (2 marks)

6. Compare the properties of magnesium oxide (metal oxide) and sulfur dioxide (non-metal oxide). (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Metal | An element that loses electrons to form positive ions |
| Non-metal | An element that gains or shares electrons |
| Metalloid | An element with properties between metals and non-metals |
| Malleable | Can be hammered into shape |
| Ductile | Can be drawn into wire |
| Semiconductor | A material with conductivity between metals and insulators |

## Summary

**Metals:**
- Left side of periodic table
- Shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors
- Lose electrons, form positive ions
- Basic oxides

**Non-metals:**
- Right side of periodic table
- Dull, brittle, poor conductors (usually)
- Gain/share electrons, form negative ions or covalent bonds
- Acidic oxides

**Metalloids:**
- Along the staircase line
- Intermediate properties
- Semiconductors (useful in electronics)

**The differences are due to:**
- Metallic bonding (free electrons) vs covalent bonding (no free electrons)
- Structure determines properties
